title: Each day a whole life
hookLine: treat each day as if it were a complete life

lines: WHAT IF IT WERE THE WHOLE SHOW?
cards: Most days don't feel complete. They feel like episodes in a long series: a lot of setup, some unfinished business, and to be continued at the bottom. Most nights end with half the plot still hanging.

The second half of Seneca's twelfth letter flips that feeling. What if each day were not an episode, but the whole show? To make it stick, he tells a very strange story about a Roman governor's dinner parties.

teach.b: Life is made of parts, Seneca says, like circles inside circles. A whole life is the biggest.
Inside it are the years, the months, and at the center the smallest circle, a single day, with its own beginning and end, its morning and evening.

teach.h: ARRANGE EACH DAY AS IF COMPLETE.
teach.b: He quotes the old philosopher Heraclitus: one day is equal to every day. So every day should be arranged as if it were the last in the line, as if it rounded off and completed our life. Not in a panic.
In order. Then the strange story. A Roman official named Pacuvius, who governed Syria for years, held a kind of funeral for himself every evening.
After dinner, with wine and ceremony, he had himself carried from the table to bed while his servants chanted, in Greek: he has lived, he has lived. Seneca admits Pacuvius did it out of bad habits.
But let's do it, he says, from a good conscience. When we go to sleep, let's be able to say gladly: I have lived.
And the best part: if tomorrow comes, take it as a bonus. Whoever can say I have lived gets up each morning to a gain. This isn't gloom.
A day that's whole doesn't need tomorrow to rescue it, and a tomorrow that arrives anyway is pure gift, unwrapped at sunrise.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism review each evening as if the day were a whole life, tying up what they can, and greet the next morning as a gift.

o: a Greek who said one day is equal to every day

a Roman poet who wrote songs for funeral feasts

games.q: each day a whole life — tap the pairs.
p: one day is equal to every day

s: Seneca admired Pacuvius as a model of virtue
he says Pacuvius did it from bad habits; we should do it from a good conscience.
Seneca quotes Heraclitus: one day is equal to every day
a day, like a life, has a beginning and an end.
Seneca's point is to live each day in fear that it's the last
it's to make each day complete, and take tomorrow as a gain.

games.q: you're Seneca. you've just told the odd story of Pacuvius' nightly mock funeral. what lesson do you draw from it?
o: end each day able to say gladly, I have lived.
games.why: Pacuvius did it from bad habits; Seneca says let's do it from a good conscience, and treat tomorrow as a bonus.

practice: Picture tonight, the moment you lie down, and look back over the day as if it were a whole life: a morning, its work, its people, its evening.
Ask what would make it feel complete, not perfect: one call, one thing finished, one thank you. Then let the words rest in you quietly: I have lived.

wordCard.voice: Pacuvius. The Roman official who held a nightly funeral for himself, so he could say: I have lived. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a whole life. Tomorrow, if it comes, is a bonus. Day four hundred forty-seven, done.
